definition: Laceration means a deep cut or tear in flesh.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word laceration. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know laceration should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The chef's knife slipped, leaving a laceration across her palm that needed immediate attention.
A nick is a tiny, shallow cut that barely bleeds — far less serious than a laceration.
Mutilation is far more extreme than a laceration: severe, disfiguring damage to the body.

A gash is a long, deep cut, and the word is vivid and informal — you can almost see the wound gape. Laceration names the same class of injury in clinical language: the word paramedics radio in and doctors write on charts. A camper complains of a gash; the ER records a laceration.

A slash is a cut named for the stroke that made it: one long, sweeping motion, usually from a blade. A laceration is named for the wound itself — a deep cut or tear in flesh, however it happened — so a ragged tear from rock or sheet metal is a laceration but never a slash.

Laceration means a deep cut or tear in flesh.
Halfway up the ridge, Dana's foot slipped and her forearm dragged across a sharp flake of granite.
The rock tore through her sleeve and opened the skin below.
At the trailhead clinic, the doctor irrigated the wound, then closed the laceration with eight stitches.
She would climb again, but the scar would stay.
The torn-open wound that needed stitches — not a bruise or a light scrape — is what makes Dana's injury a laceration.
Laceration is the word doctors and first responders use for a cut or tear in flesh.

Keep it apart from grievous (another word in this unit): a laceration is one specific physical injury, while grievous describes how severe any harm is — a laceration can be grievous, but grievous harm need not involve a cut at all.

On the first morning of the wilderness medicine course, the instructor held up a photograph of a climber's forearm and asked the class what they saw.
The instructor shook her head: in the backcountry, she said, precision saves time, and time saves tissue.
The photo showed a laceration — deep, ragged, and past the reach of a simple bandage.
The distinction matters over a radio.
A rescue coordinator who hears the precise word knows to send sutures, irrigation kits, and a litter team.
Students spent the afternoon practicing the vocabulary of wounds along with the treatment, learning to describe depth, edges, and bleeding in the fewest possible words.
By the final drill, no one said "a cut." The reports came back measured and exact, and the mock rescues ran twice as fast.
